opener.heading: Week 3: Kindness & Community 💛
about: Most of the kindness around Azlyn happens out of her sight. The shopping arrives, the heating comes on, somebody made the dinner. This week she does it herself seven times over: a verse for every person in the house, a show for an audience of one, bird cakes for a frozen January, three real jobs before lunch, soup for the neighbors, a box of her own toys given away, cookies and cards on Thursday. One thread runs under all of it. The Good Thing Jar goes on the kitchen table on Friday and takes a paper strip every time somebody here does something for somebody else, and nobody reads a single strip until Day 21.

Martin Luther King Jr. Day lands on Monday, and Day 18 marks it with work. She gets three jobs she can finish before lunch and a pot of soup after it, and half of that pot leaves the house before dinner. Azlyn chooses which house it goes to and carries the jar to the door herself.
azlyn: Making up a verse to a tune she knows. Holding the beat, feeling where the line has to land, and getting words there before the bar runs out.
Running a show start to finish. Waiting behind a curtain, coming out on her name, doing three items in the order she chose, and ending it.
Real jobs with a real result. Six potatoes scrubbed go in the soup, socks come back as pairs, soft vegetables get cut with a table knife she controls.
Choosing what to give and handing it over. A toy box into a stranger's hands, a jar of soup next door, cookies on three doorsteps.
Plain words for how people look. Skin, hair and eyes named out loud, and a crayon found for her own arm, yours and Kreston's.
you: Verses she invents are worth more than verses she repeats
Performing for one person is enough
Kindness has to be visible before it can be learned
The age where they want to help is right now, and it's brief
Giving feels good only when the child does the giving
Children notice difference early, and silence teaches something
Gratitude is a skill, and it starts with noticing

opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 7 months this week. He reaches across his own body for something sitting on his far side, moves it from hand to hand, and babbles in long strings that run like sentences.

days.title: The Made-Up Song
days.prepTonight: Put four sheets of paper, a pen and three wooden spoons on the table with a saucepan and a small plastic tub upside down beside them, and wash and dry a jar with a lid for the afternoon.

opening.title: Who the Song Is For
opening.need: paper, 4–5 sheets · 1 pen · the kitchen table.
steps: Ask her to name everyone who lives in this house. Write one name at the top of each sheet in big letters and let her choose which comes first.
Pick the tune. Twinkle Twinkle, Frère Jacques, Happy Birthday, anything she sings unprompted. Sing it once with the words it came with.
Ask her one true thing about the first person. Write the answer under the name. That line opens the song at 9:15.

main.title: A Verse for Each Person
materials: 1 saucepan and a second wooden spoon as a drum
Your phone, to record one take
steps: Sing the tune you chose this morning once with her name in it, so she hears the shape before she has to make one.
Hand her the spoon and take the first sheet. Say the name at the top and let her sing. Write it down word for word, wrong grammar included.
Keep a slow beat on the upturned saucepan underneath her. The beat carries her over the gap where the words run out.
Work through every sheet. Do not offer her a rhyme and do not tidy a line she has sung. Kreston's verse will be about his feet.
Read the whole thing back as one song and put her own name in the last line.
Record one take on your phone. One. Sing it again afterwards with your hands free.
main.tip: She will change the words on the second singing and be certain the new ones were always there. Write those underneath instead of correcting her. Both versions are hers.

outside.title: The Singing Walk
paras: Take the song out and sing it down the street. Cold January air carries a voice further than she expects, and she will hear her own noise come back off the houses. Sing your verse first so she sees a grown adult do it outdoors. Let her pick who gets a verse: a dog, a parked van, the woman at the bus stop.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months and babbling in long strings now, which is singing with the words still missing. Sit him on the floor with a wooden spoon of his own and the upturned plastic tub while Azlyn works. He bangs it, and the noise lands in the middle of her song instead of beside it. Set the spoon down on his far side once or twice, because reaching across his own body is new this month and worth the stretch.

second.title: The Good Thing Jar
second.intro: The jar lands on the kitchen table today and stays all week. Good things go in on paper strips, and on Thursday you tip the lot out and read them.
materials: 1 clean jar with a lid, or a plastic tub
steps: Give her the empty jar and the crayons and leave her to decorate it. Tape covers a lot. So do stickers.
Write THE GOOD THING JAR on a strip of tape and let her stick it on crooked.
Cut the paper into strips together. Twenty is plenty and thirty is better.
Walk the house room by room. In each room, name one thing somebody did for somebody else today: the tea you made, the toy Azlyn handed Kreston, the door Joseph shut.
Write each one on a strip, read it out loud, and hand it to her to post. She posts every strip.
Do three strips about her without using the word good or the word girl. Name the action: Azlyn carried the basket to the door.
Put the jar where she can reach it. Anybody can post one, any time, and nobody reads them until Thursday.
second.tip: Write what the person did, never what the person is. "Azlyn shared the cookie" is something she can do again tomorrow. "Azlyn is kind" is a verdict, and a verdict is harder to live with.

alternatives: Decorate the jar, post one strip, and leave the week to fill it.
Draw the good things instead of writing them, one per strip.
Post strips for people outside the house: grandparents, the woman at the store.
Tape a paper chain to the wall and add a link for each one.
outAgain: Playgroup, and the song goes with her if she wants an audience
A friend's house, one child, one hour
The park, for whoever needs the noise taken out of them
A café with a window seat and one hot drink you get to finish
The corner store, and she carries the basket to the register

aroundWorld.title: Southern Africa & Ubuntu 💛
paras: The Nguni languages of southern Africa carry a word for the idea that a person is made a person by other people: ubuntu. The full saying, umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu, comes out in English as "a person is a person through other people." Desmond Tutu spent years explaining it to audiences who wanted a one-word translation, and no single English word holds it.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Cook one pot tonight and stand it in the middle of the table. Everyone serves themselves from the same dish, Azlyn included, and she passes the spoon on.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: In Zulu, hello is sawubona, and it means "I see you."

days.krestonPM: Cut him two or three strips from thicker paper and let him crumple them while Azlyn posts hers. At 7 months he moves a thing from one hand to the other and back, and paper that crackles holds him longer than a toy that stays silent. Keep his strips too big for his mouth.

insight.headline: Verses she invents are worth more than verses she repeats.
paras: Azlyn can sing back a nursery rhyme she has heard two hundred times, and that is memory doing its work. Making up a verse asks for something harder. She has to hold the tune, feel where the beats fall, and land a line that fits before the bar runs out. Adults pay for lessons in that. She does it at three because nobody has told her it is difficult. Writing the lines down changes the transaction, because the words she pulled out of nothing now exist on paper and get read back to her. Children who invent language rather than recite it build a stronger sense of what words can do.

days.safety: A glass jar carried by a three-year-old with Kreston on the floor is a bad combination. Use a plastic tub, or keep the jar on the table and let her post the strips standing up. Loose paper goes in his mouth, so sweep before you put him down.

days.title: The Show for One
days.prepTonight: Find a sheet or thin blanket for a curtain, dig out six clothespins and the flashlight, and stand two dining chairs either side of the kitchen doorway.

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Forks and the Water Cups

opening.title: The One Ticket
opening.need: card or a cereal box · crayons · scissors (yours) · 1 pen.
steps: Tell her a show is happening at 1:00 and one ticket exists. She decides who gets it.
Cut a rectangle of card and hand it over. The picture on the front is whatever the show will be about, so she chooses that too.
Write ADMIT ONE along the bottom and let her copy the shapes underneath. It stands against the kettle until she walks it round at 10:30.

main.title: The Kitchen Stage
materials: 1 sheet or thin blanket for the curtain
Card and crayons for a sign
steps: Stand a chair either side of the doorway, backs facing into the room, and clip the sheet across both backs so it hangs as a curtain she can drag aside. You hang it, she tells you it is crooked.
Put the cushion on the floor a few paces back. The auditorium seats one.
Ask her what the show is. Take the first three answers and write them on the card in order: a song, a dance, a jump off the bottom stair.
Rehearse the opening on its own. She waits behind the sheet, you say her name, she pulls the curtain and comes out. Do it four times. The coming out is the part she is learning.
Run all three items once in order with the flashlight on her from the cushion.
Stop while she still wants more. The show is at 1:00.
main.tip: Resist adding a fourth item. Three things she can hold in her head beat six she has to be reminded of, and a show she runs unprompted is one she owns.

outside.title: Posting the Invitation
paras: Take the ticket off the kettle and walk it to whoever is coming at 1:00. If the audience lives in this house, she posts it through your own front door and you act surprised when it lands on the mat. A grandparent up the road means the whole walk, with the mail slot flap hers to push. Gloves on. January makes that flap colder than she expects.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months, and a curtain that opens and shuts is the best offer he has had all week. Sit him at the audience end and let Azlyn drag the sheet across and back. He holds onto the idea of a thing after it leaves his sight, and every pull tests that. Keep the sheet clear of his face.

second.title: The One-Person Show
second.intro: At one o'clock the ticket holder sits down, and everybody else in the house is either backstage or out of the room.
materials: 2 cookies and a drink for the audience
Your phone, to film one song
steps: Seat the audience. One cushion, one person, cookies and a drink in their hands. Nobody watches from the doorway.
Take the delivered ticket at the door and tear the corner off. She will care about this more than any other thirty seconds of the afternoon.
Announce her by her full name from behind the curtain, then get out of the way. Flashlight on, big light off.
Watch the whole thing. No correcting the running order, no feeding her the words. Clap after each item.
Ask for one of them again. An encore from an audience of one is the point of the afternoon.
Swap over. She takes the cushion and the second cookie, you go behind the curtain and do a song.
Leave the stage up. She runs the show again at 4:15 with nobody watching, and that version belongs to her.
second.tip: Film one song at the start, then put the phone face down. She can tell a parent watching from a parent recording, and she plays to the room she is given.

alternatives: One song from behind the sofa. Same idea, four minutes.
A puppet show over a chair back with two socks.
She directs and you perform the whole thing.
Call a grandparent and do the show over the phone.
outAgain: The farm, for the indoor barn and whatever gets fed at three
Indoor playground, if the farm has turned to mud
The park, and the show gets performed again on the climbing frame
A friend's house, and a second audience of one
The pet store, twenty minutes, nothing bought
days.krestonPM: He goes to the farm in the carrier, where at 7 months the smell of a barn is new information and he goes quiet in it because he is working. Keep him clear of anything with teeth and wash both pairs of hands before anybody eats. Back home he gets the hairbrush microphone, and the shouting into it is aimed at a person now.

insight.headline: Performing for one person is enough.
paras: A three-year-old singing to a room of adults is doing a different job from a three-year-old singing to one. The audience of one keeps her attention on the thing itself, on the song and the order and the ending she planned, with no crowd to read. She gets the whole arc: waiting behind a curtain, starting, finishing, watched the entire way through. Children build social confidence in doses about this size. One person who stays until the end teaches her that a thing has a finish, and that finishing it is the good part. Two people watching is not twice as good to her. It is twice as much to keep track of.

days.safety: She will climb on a dining chair to reach the curtain. You hang it, she stands back. Nothing tied at neck height, no cord left running across the doorway, and no draped sheet anywhere over Kreston. Take the curtain down before bed.

days.title: Feeding the Birds
days.prepTonight: Take the lard out to soften overnight and put the yogurt pots, the birdseed and three feet of string beside it.

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Forks and the Crumb Pot

opening.title: The Window Count
opening.need: the window with the best view · paper · 1 crayon · two chairs.
steps: Pull the chairs up to the glass and sit with her before the house is awake.
Every bird that lands in view gets a mark on the paper. She makes the mark, you keep still. Count them out loud at the end.
Ask her where a bird finds food in January with the ground frozen. Do not answer. You are making some at 9:15.

main.title: The Bird Cakes
materials: 250 g lard or solid vegetable fat, left out to soften (smooth peanut butter works instead)
500 g birdseed, or rolled oats, breadcrumbs, raisins and sunflower seeds mixed
4–6 clean yogurt pots or empty cans
1 large mixing bowl and 1 wooden spoon
1 skewer or the point of the scissors, adult only, for the string hole
steps: Make a hole in the base of each pot with the skewer, thread a loop of string through and knot it inside. Yours to do, and she counts the pots.
Tip the softened fat into the bowl and let her get both hands in it. It takes her a minute to commit.
Add the seed, oats, crumbs and raisins a scoop at a time and let her squeeze until the mix holds in a lump. One part fat to two parts dry, by eye.
Pack the mix into the pots and let her press it down with her fists, string held out of the way.
Into the fridge to set. They come out at 1:00.
Wash both pairs of hands with soap before you touch the counter.
main.tip: Let her overfill one pot and underfill another. Birds have no standards, and the two she got wrong are the two she watches hardest.

outside.title: Where the Birds Are
paras: Walk the usual route with one job: find where the birds already are. In January they cluster in thick hedges, in anything with berries still on it, and in the tangle at the back of a yard. Stand still under a hedge for a minute and listen before either of you looks up. Let her choose the branch the cakes hang from on the way home.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months. Hold him up to the glass before you go out, tap where a bird lands and wait. He follows a pointing finger on a good day and stares at the finger on a bad one. Outside, stop the stroller under the hedge and let him turn his head toward a sound with nothing attached to it.

second.title: The Feeding Station
second.intro: The cakes come out of the fridge set hard, and the afternoon happens at the window under a blanket.
materials: 1 shallow dish, an old plant saucer or a takeout lid
A pitcher of warm water to thaw the dish
Paper and 1 crayon for the tally
steps: Run warm water round the outside of each pot and the cake slides out whole. Leave a long loop of string.
Hang them where she can see them from the chair: low branches, the clothesline, a nail in the fence. She picks the spots, you tie the knots.
Stand the shallow dish in the open, clear of any bush a cat could sit under, and pour the warm water in. Unfrozen water in January is harder to find than food.
Scatter crumbs on the ground for the birds that will not use a feeder.
Come in, pull the chair to the window and get under the blanket. The wait outlasts her patience on day one.
Every arrival gets a mark on the tally, same as 8:00. Put the two sheets side by side at the end.
Leave the tally and the crayon on the windowsill. She keeps marking it all week with nobody asking.
second.tip: Twenty minutes of nothing is the normal result. Name the birds you both know, then let the quiet come back. A hide with a commentary running in it stops being a hide.

alternatives: Hang one cake and put the water dish out.
Thread cereal hoops onto string and hang those instead.
Draw the birds she saw this morning from memory.
Press crumbs into an apple core and spike it on a twig.
outAgain: The scooter or the balance bike, helmet on, to the end of the road and back
The park, counting birds there and back
A long loop with the stroller and no destination
Feed the ducks with the crusts she has been saving
The pet store and its seed aisle, if it is too wet to be out
days.krestonPM: He faces Azlyn in the stroller while she scoots, so turn the seat round. At 7 months he tracks a moving thing across his whole field of view, and a sister on wheels is the best one going. Back at the window he sits on your lap and slaps the glass, which is a fair contribution to the tally.

insight.headline: Kindness has to be visible before it can be learned.
paras: Azlyn cannot see most of the kindness around her. The shopping arrives, the heating comes on, and none of it looks to her like a choice anybody made. Feeding birds in January puts one act of care in front of her start to finish. The need is real, the animal is cold, and she is the one with her hands in the fat. Children copy what they can watch being done more than what they are told about, and a dish of thawed water on a frozen morning is a kindness with all its working shown.

days.safety: Loose birdseed on the floor near a seven-month-old who mouths everything, so sweep before you put Kreston down. Wash both pairs of hands after handling seed, fat and feeders. Use smooth peanut butter only, never whole or chopped nuts, and check for a nut allergy before you start. Keep the bird dish shallow and stand it where you can see it from the window, and tip it out before you put Kreston down anywhere near it, because a baby drowns in less water than that.

days.title: The Helping Day
days.prepTonight: Leave the sock basket unsorted, put the bowl, the stool, the brush and six potatoes by the sink, and find a jar with a screw lid.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath and a Story About Dr King

opening.title: The Job Board
opening.need: 1 sheet of paper · 1 pen · crayons · masking tape.
steps: Draw three boxes down a sheet of paper and let her fill each with a picture of the job: the potatoes, the socks, the windows.
Tape it to the kitchen door at her height, not yours.
Tell her all three are real, all three are hers, and nobody else is doing them today. She picks which goes first.

main.title: Three Real Jobs
steps: The potatoes. Bowl of warm water on the towel, stool beside it, brush in her hand. Six scrubbed until the water goes brown, and she decides when one is finished.
The socks. Tip the basket out and let her hunt for pairs. She will put a black one with a navy one, and those two go in the drawer as a pair.
The windows. Spray bottle in one hand, cloth in the other, one low window or the back door glass. Smears are the finish.
Hand each job over and move away from it. Ten minutes each is slow, and she has the whole hour.
Say what she did rather than how it turned out. "The potatoes are washed and they go in the soup at 1:00" attaches the job to something.
Do not redo any of it where she can see you. The window can wait.
main.tip: Every job has to be one she can finish. A whole basket of socks is a wall. The same basket with the whites pulled out has an end on it.

outside.title: Taking the Trash Cans In
paras: Monday, and the trash cans are out. Wheel yours back down the path with her hands on the handle beside yours, then knock next door and bring theirs in too. She holds on and does almost none of the pulling, and she knows it. Walk the block after and let her pick up three pieces of litter with a bag over her hand.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months and copies the shape of a job long before he can do one. Sit him on the towel with a dry cloth of his own and a wooden spoon, a full arm's length clear of the water. Raw potato breaks off in hard pieces under a gum, so the potatoes stay on her side. He bangs the spoon, hands it to you and waits for it back, which is the game of his month.

second.title: Soup for Two Houses
second.intro: Today is Martin Luther King Jr. Day, marked by doing something for somebody else. Half of this pot leaves the house before dinner.
materials: 1 onion, 3 carrots, the 6 potatoes she scrubbed this morning
1 zucchini or a handful of mushrooms, soft for her knife
1 can of chopped tomatoes or 2 bouillon cubes
1 table knife and 1 chopping board for her
1 clean jar with a screw lid
steps: Set her up at the table with the board, the table knife and the soft vegetables. The hard ones are yours.
Show her the grip once: fingers curled back, other hand flat on the blade, push down and forward. Then let her do it her own way.
Everything she cuts goes in the pot, including the pieces the size of her fist. Soup forgives.
Onto the stovetop with the tomatoes, the stock and the water. She stirs from the stool with your hand over hers, pan handle turned in.
Thirty minutes of simmering, and in the gap she chooses which house gets the jar.
Ladle half in once it has stopped steaming, screw the lid down, wrap the dish towel round it and hand it to her.
Deliver it before dinner, or call ahead and take it tomorrow. She hands it over herself.
second.tip: Do not give her a line to say at the door. Whatever comes out will be better than anything you could have written.

alternatives: Sandwiches instead of soup, and half of them go next door.
She washes and you cook, and the whole pot stays here.
Bag up cans she chooses for the food bank.
Draw a card for the person getting the jar.
outAgain: The woods loop, muddy in January and better for it
The riverside path, to see how high the water is
The neighborhood park, twenty minutes, then home to the pot
A drive to drop the jar off, with her holding it
The indoor play center, if the woods have washed out
days.krestonPM: He goes in the carrier for the woods, facing out. At 7 months he grabs everything within reach, so keep low branches away from his hands and check what comes back in his fist. He stays out of the kitchen while the pot is on the stovetop, and gets the empty can and a wooden spoon once it is off.

insight.headline: The age where they want to help is right now, and it's brief.
paras: Azlyn wants the brush, the cloth and the spray bottle, because the work is real and she has watched you do it. Toddlers offer help without being asked from around eighteen months, and the offers thin out across the school years as the help keeps getting turned down for being slow. She scrubs six potatoes in the time you would take over twenty, and those six go in the pot in front of her. Take the offer while she is still making it, and let the standard be hers. The potatoes will come out with grit still on them. The offer is worth more this month than the potatoes are.

days.safety: The dishpan holds enough water to drown Kreston at 7 months, so he stays inside arm's reach of you the whole time it is down and it gets tipped out every time you step away from it. Hot pot on the stovetop with a three-year-old at counter height: pan handles turned in, she stirs from the stool with your hand on hers, and the soup goes into the jar cool enough to hold. The knives you use stay out of reach between cuts.

days.title: Giving It Away
days.prepTonight: Put a strong box and two sturdy bags at the bottom of the stairs, dig out a shoebox and any thick cardboard for the afternoon, and pack the swim bag.

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Forks and the Swim Bag

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath and the Book She Kept

opening.title: Keep or Give
opening.need: 8 of her own toys · a clear bit of floor · nothing else.
steps: Bring eight things she owns into the middle of the floor. You choose them, and pick ones she has not touched in a month.
Two piles: keep and give. She decides every one and you say nothing.
If all eight land in keep, that is the answer and you carry on. Tell her the box is going to a child who has none of this, and leave it there.

main.title: The Giving Box
materials: Paper and 1 pen for her list
steps: Start with clothes. Anything she has grown out of comes off the shelf, and she holds each thing once before it goes in.
Move on to toys. She chooses. You get one veto for the whole morning, so hold onto it.
She wipes every item with the damp cloth before it goes in. She is sending these out in good condition and her hands do that part.
Anything broken goes in the separate bag. Broken things are trash, and she gets to be the one who says which is which.
Ask her for one line about each toy, meant for the child who gets it. Write it word for word on a strip of tape and stick it on: THIS ONE ROLLS DOWN THE STAIRS.
Tape the box shut, let her draw on the lid, and stand it by the front door where she walks past it.
main.tip: She will pull one thing back out of the box. Let her, and say nothing about it. A child who is allowed to take one thing back puts three more in.

outside.title: Delivering the Box
paras: The box goes today, while it still means something to her. Load it into the bottom of the stroller and walk it to the thrift store, the church porch or the family two streets over with a smaller child. Let her carry it the last twenty feet even though it is too big for her, and hand it across herself. Ask whoever takes it to tell her where it goes next.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months and everything in that box has been in his mouth at some point, so wipe as you pack. Give him one toy that is staying, a soft one of Azlyn's she has agreed to lend for the morning, and watch what happens when she takes it back. He does not mind yet. That window shuts somewhere around his first birthday.

second.title: Kreston's Posting Box
second.intro: Something arrives in the house this afternoon instead of leaving it, and Azlyn makes it for her brother.
materials: Thick cardboard cut into discs the size of your palm, 8–10
1 scarf or wide ribbon to thread through and pull out
steps: Cut three or four hand-sized holes in the lid and one bigger one in the side. The scissors are yours throughout.
Cut the cardboard into discs the size of your palm, eight to ten, counted out loud so she knows the number you started with.
Hand her the crayons and the marker. Every disc gets decorated and so does the box. Write KRESTON on the lid in outline for her to fill in.
Thread the scarf through the side hole so a hand's length hangs out, no more. He pulls, it keeps coming, and he comes back to it all afternoon.
Show her how to post a disc through the lid, then hand the box over and let her teach him. You stay out of it.
Sit behind them both and watch his hands. Posting is months beyond him, and the discs are still worth having.
Count the discs back in at the end. The same number that went out.
second.tip: Let her post the discs herself for the first ten minutes before he gets a look in. She spent the morning giving her own things away, and first go on his new toy is a fair trade.

alternatives: Cut one hole, decorate the box, and call it done.
Make him a ribbon pull from an old wipes tub instead.
Draw a picture for the child who gets the giving box.
Sort what is left on her shelf into rows and stop there.
outAgain: Swimming, and she carries her own bag in
Indoor playground if the pool session is canceled
The library, a day early, for something to read in the bath
A warm café and a window, if the morning has used everybody up
The indoor play center
days.krestonPM: He comes to the pool if he is coming. At 7 months he sits supported in the water and slaps at it with both hands, and he aims the splash at a person now. Twenty minutes, then out and dressed before he goes cold.

insight.headline: Giving feels good only when the child does the giving.
paras: Sorting her toys while she is at playgroup and dropping the bag off yourself clears the cupboard. Azlyn takes nothing from it, because she was not in the room. The good feeling arrives through the doing: choosing it, holding it one last time, walking it to a door and putting it into a stranger's hands. Researchers who watch toddlers hand over treats find the pleasure shows up when the child does the handing, and less of it when the treat was never hers. She needs the whole sequence, including the part where it costs her something.

days.safety: Everything that goes in Kreston's box has to be bigger than his fist. No bottle caps, no coins, no small lids. Cut the discs palm-sized, count them in and out, and the scissors stay with you. The scarf comes out of the box the moment you stop watching. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: Same and Different
days.prepTonight: Tip the whole crayon box out on the table, browns and pinks included, and text the three people she is calling at 1:00.

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Forks and the Book Bag

opening.title: Hands on the Table
opening.need: the kitchen table · her hands, yours and Kreston's · 1 hand mirror.
steps: Lay your hand flat on the table next to hers and ask what she notices. Take whatever answer arrives, including none.
Bring Kreston's hand in and put all three side by side. Name the differences with nothing softened: bigger, smaller, darker, paler, more freckles.
Hold the mirror so she sees her own face with yours beside it. Use the words skin, hair and eyes and let her use them back.

main.title: Finding the Right Crayon
materials: The whole crayon box, browns and pinks included
Photos on your phone of the people she names
steps: Tip the whole box out. Every color on the table, nothing sorted, nothing put back.
She holds crayons against her own forearm one at a time until she finds the closest match. The hunting takes longer than you expect and it is the work.
Do the same on your arm, then on Kreston's. Three people, three crayons, and she picks all three.
Line the three up on the paper and let her see how close together they sit.
Open the photos on your phone. She names people she knows and picks a crayon for each: grandparents, the girl from playgroup, the man at the store counter.
She draws everybody in the colors she chose. Write the names on for her and put one on the fridge before lunch.
main.tip: If she decides somebody's color is wrong, agree that skin comes in more colors than the box holds, and show her how to lay two crayons over each other.

outside.title: The Hello Walk
paras: Walk with one job: say hello to every person you pass and keep score of how many say it back. A Wednesday morning in mid-January hands you dog walkers and the mail carrier, so go where the people are: the row of stores, the bus stop, the school pickup line at eleven. She does the hello with you a step behind her, and she counts the answers on her fingers.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months and studies a face that does not look like the four he sees every day. Point him at people instead of the road. Babies his age hold a gaze longer on a new face, the first version of the noticing Azlyn is doing on paper. Back home, hold him in front of the mirror with Azlyn beside him.

second.title: Three Phone Calls
second.intro: Three people are expecting a call from Azlyn this afternoon. She calls each one and asks the same three questions.
materials: 3 people agreed and warned in advance
steps: Choose the three questions together and write them big enough for her to see while she talks: What did you have for breakfast? What is the weather like? What made you laugh today?
Get on the sofa under the blanket, phone on speaker, her drawings on her lap and the crayons within reach.

Call the first one. She says hello, a long silence follows, and the person at the other end has been warned to wait through it. She asks the questions in her own order and forgets the third: prompt once, then leave it.
Write each answer down as it comes and read the three back to her once you have hung up.
She holds her drawing of that person up to the phone, which makes no sense and matters to her. Tell them what she drew, then she starts a fresh drawing of whoever is next while the number rings.
Lay the three sheets side by side once the calls are done and find the one thing all three people said. There is always one.
Turn each sheet over and let her draw what she was told: the weather at their window, the breakfast, the thing that made them laugh.
second.tip: Three questions, thirty seconds each, and nobody asks her how preschool is going. A phone call with a job inside it is one she can do. If she is still going at two, she calls a fourth.

alternatives: One call instead of three, and she draws while it happens.
Record a voice message for each person instead of calling.
Mail the drawings to all three instead of calling.
outAgain: The library, every two weeks, with her own book bag both ways
Indoor playground, if the library has a school group in
The store, and she chooses one thing off the list
The park on the way home, ten minutes, coats on
A café and the first new book read cover to cover
days.krestonPM: He goes down in the library's picture-book corner. At 7 months he reads a board book by getting a corner into his mouth and turning it over. Hunt out books with real photographs of faces, hold one in front of him and see which face he stays with longest. Azlyn chooses his second one.

insight.headline: Children notice difference early, and silence teaches something.
paras: Azlyn clocked skin color around her second birthday and has sorted people by it ever since, the same way she sorts crayons and socks. Saying nothing feels neutral from the inside. Children read an adult's silence as a signal that a subject is off limits, then fill the gap with an explanation of their own. Naming what she sees, in plain words with none of your anxiety in it, hands her the language before she invents worse for herself. The crayon she chose for her own arm and the one she chose for Kreston are different, and both drawings are on the fridge.

days.safety: The hand mirror is glass, so keep it in your hand or use a plastic one, and put it away when you finish. Crayons go off the floor while Kreston is down, because a snapped one is mouth-sized. The phone stays out of his reach between calls.

days.title: Thank You Day
days.prepTonight: Take the butter out to soften, set the tray, the rolling pin and a cutter beside it, and stand the Good Thing Jar in the middle of the table.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Cutters and the Dough Scraps

opening.title: Reading the Jar
opening.need: the Good Thing Jar · the strips · the kitchen table.
steps: Tip the whole jar out and let her push the strips around with both hands. There should be twenty or more.
Read every one out loud. All of them, including the four that say the same thing.
Sort them into piles, one per person, and count each pile out loud. That count is how many cookies get cut at 9:15.

main.title: Thank-You Cookies
materials: 300 g all-purpose flour, plus extra for the board
1 cooling rack or a cold plate
steps: Butter and sugar in the bowl, flour on top. She rubs it through with her fingertips until the bowl looks like breadcrumbs. Both hands in, no spoon.
Add the milk a spoon at a time and let her squeeze it into a dough. A dusting of flour fixes it if it sticks to her.
Flour the board and roll it out to about a finger's thickness. Leave the thin patches where they are.
She counts the shapes against the piles from 8:00 and keeps cutting until the numbers match. Re-roll the scraps twice, then the third lot is hers.
Bake at 350°F for 12 to 15 minutes, until the edges turn gold. She stays at the table. You move the tray.
Slide them onto the cold plate once they firm up, and count them again with her when they are cool.
main.tip: Let her cut whatever shapes she wants. Somebody is getting a triangle with a thumbprint in it, and that person is getting the better cookie.

outside.title: The Cookie Round
paras: Bag the cookies in twos and walk them round. The neighbor who took the package in, the woman at the corner store, the friend who has had a rough month. She knocks, she hands them over, she says her own version of the words. Ten minutes a stop, so pick three doors and stop at three. Keep two back for the walk home.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months and the kitchen at 9:15 is hot, floury and no place for him. Set him up in the doorway with a wooden spoon and the saucepan, out of the kitchen and in your sight, and keep the flour bag off the floor because it goes straight in his mouth. On the round, wariness of an unfamiliar face is new this month, so keep him facing you when somebody leans in.

second.title: The Thank-You Cards
second.intro: Every strip in that jar has a name on it, and every one of those people gets a card this afternoon.
materials: Card, or cereal boxes cut into rectangles, 8–10
1 stamp, if one is going in the mail
steps: Cut the card into rectangles and fold them. Cereal boxes work fine and the printed side goes on the inside.
Take the strips one person at a time. Read them out loud, then ask her what the card should say.
Write her words down word for word. THANK YOU FOR CARRYING ME UP THE STAIRS WHEN MY LEGS WERE TIRED. Do not shorten it or fix the grammar.
She draws the thing they did on the front. The drawing will be unrecognizable and the person will recognize it, because her words sit underneath.
She signs each one: a shape, a letter A, a single line, the same mark on every card so it becomes her signature.
Stickers and glue on whatever needs them, then stack the finished cards next to the cookie bags by the door.
One card goes in the mail with a stamp on it. Walk to the mailbox before dinner and let her drop it in.
second.tip: Do the cards for the people in this house last, and find a reason to leave the room when she gets to yours.

alternatives: Three cards instead of ten, and the rest wait for the weekend.
She dictates and you write, no drawing at all.
Print a photo of each person and glue it on the front.
Make one enormous card and everybody signs it.
outAgain: The market, late on, when the stalls are selling off what is left
The bakery, and she picks the thing for after dinner
The post office, if the card missed the mail this morning
The park, for whatever the oven and the doorsteps left in her
The corner store and the long way home past the mailbox
days.krestonPM: Take him to the market in the carrier facing out and stop at one loud or bright stall. At 7 months he babbles in long runs and a busy street pulls it out of him, so answer him as though he said words. Give him a lidded can or an unopened box to hold while Azlyn hands the money over. Raw apple and raw carrot break off in hard pieces, so neither goes in his hands.

insight.headline: Gratitude is a skill, and it starts with noticing.
paras: Prompting say thank you teaches Azlyn a word to produce on cue. The jar teaches the step underneath the word. All week she has watched for the things people did and heard them written down, so by Thursday she can name eleven of them. The noticing is the part that carries. A child who works out what somebody did for her, and then does something back, holds onto it longer than one reminded to be polite. She made a cookie for each name, and that is a thank you with a cost inside it. Her list will have the mail carrier on it and leave you off. Write it down the way she says it.

days.safety: The oven is on and the tray comes out at her eye level. She stays back from the door, the hot tray goes to the middle of the counter, and Kreston stays out of the kitchen while it moves. Raw dough is not a snack today.
